anchorClaim: In low-income countries from 2010-2020, reductions of 20% or more in international vaccine funding correlate at r>=0.5 with declines in national vaccination coverage rates within 2 years.
confidenceSummary: This is a genuine shortage of evidence, not a finding: DATOM located only a few studies, none of which directly measures vaccine funding levels against coverage, so there is not yet enough here to judge the claim either way.
dataQualityNote: Only 4 real datoms exist for this claim against a sources_target of 100, a genuinely thin evidence base; the confidence_band (Speculative) and low score (0.11) reflect that honestly. None of the 4 retrieved sources directly measures the nucleus claim's specific quantitative relationship (20% funding cut correlating at r>=0.5 with coverage decline within 2 years): one paper (Berman 2004) predates the 2010-2020 study window, one (Lewnard 2020) measures vaccine effectiveness rather than funding-coverage links, one (Bruni 2020) documents a coverage-pattern trend without funding data, and one (Sbarra/LBD 2020) touches funding only as one of four co-named drivers (alongside conflict, vaccine scepticism, and supply disruption) behind a documented coverage slowdown, not as an independently tested predictor of it. Also worth flagging: the datomerId field stored on all 4 of the 4 individual datom records (44535375-36ad-4e00-9450-6b8936d9aee9 on three, f44ce3cf-a04f-4766-9d2f-db38f1800889 on one) does not match the parent Datomer's own datomerId (458642d5-4d7e-4840-89c9-081c23ccd489); linkage was confirmed instead via the Datomer's explicit datom_ids array and matching projectId (6391d547-4160-4938-bbba-ca770f16cde7), so a direct GSI query on datomerId returned zero rows.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure the correlation between international vaccine funding reductions and vaccination coverage rate declines in low-income countries during 2010-2020.
datoms.source: P. Berman. "Immunization financing in developing countries and the international vaccine market: trends and issues" (2004). doi:10.1590/S0042-96862004000900017
datoms.domain: Public health policy and immunization financing
datoms.measure: Immunization financing trends and vaccine market dynamics
datoms.notes: Published in 2004, predating the 2010-2020 window specified in the nucleus claim; does not measure the funding-coverage correlation. Sample size not reported; flagged with a statistical-reliability warning during ingestion.

datoms.claim: Low- and middle-income countries with HPV vaccination programs achieved lower final-dose coverage rates than high-income countries due to higher dropout rates between first and final doses.
datoms.source: Laia Bruni, Anna Saura-Lázaro, Alexandra Montoliu, María Brotons, Laia Alemany. "HPV vaccination introduction worldwide and WHO and UNICEF estimates of national HPV immunization coverage 2010-2019" (2020). doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2020.106399
datoms.population: Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries with HPV vaccination programs, 2010-2019
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage rates (first dose and final dose)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of WHO/UNICEF vaccination coverage estimates
datoms.notes: Addresses coverage outcomes in low-income settings but does not examine funding data or the relationship between funding reductions and coverage declines. Global population-weighted final-dose coverage was only 15% in 2019; only 6% of countries reached >90% final-dose coverage.

datoms.claim: The paper does not measure the correlation between international vaccine funding reductions and vaccination coverage declines; it measures vaccine effectiveness against antibiotic-treated illness outcomes.
datoms.source: Joseph A. Lewnard, Nathan C. Lo, Nimalan Arinaminpathy, Isabel Frost, Ramanan Laxminarayan. "Childhood vaccines and antibiotic use in low- and middle-income countries" (2020). doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2238-4
datoms.population: Children under five years of age in low- and middle-income countries
datoms.measure: Antibiotic-treated acute respiratory infection and diarrhoea episodes prevented by vaccination
datoms.methodology: Case-control study with household survey data
datoms.sample_size: 65,815 children from case-control analysis; 944,173 children across 77 countries in incidence analysis
datoms.notes: Measures vaccine effectiveness against antibiotic-treated illness, not the funding-to-coverage relationship in the nucleus claim; scored as contradicting because it is off-target to the claim rather than confirming it. Relied on mother-reported outcomes rather than standardized clinical assessment.

datoms.claim: In low-income and middle-income countries, measles vaccination coverage declined or stagnated in more than half of districts between 2010 and 2019, following gains from 2000 to 2010.
datoms.source: Local Burden of Disease Vaccine Coverage Collaborators, Alyssa N. Sbarra, Sam Rolfe, Jason Q. Nguyen, Lucas Earl. "Mapping routine measles vaccination in low- and middle-income countries" (2020). doi:10.1038/s41586-020-03043-4
datoms.population: Children aged 12-59 months in 101 low- and middle-income countries
datoms.methodology: Geostatistical modelling with Bayesian hierarchical framework
datoms.notes: Documents a slowdown in coverage progress after 2010 (70.5% of districts improving 2000-2010 versus only 40.1% in 2010-2019), which authors attribute to conflict, vaccine scepticism, funding support, and supply disruptions jointly, not funding withdrawal in isolation. Cites Angola's 28% drop in per-capita health spending (2010-2018) coinciding with coverage declines as one example among several drivers.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM found only 4 studies that speak to this claim, well short of what a question like this needs, and none was built to test whether cutting international vaccine funding actually causes coverage to fall. So the record stays open: the honest answer today is that there is not enough evidence to judge it either way. That is what the "Insufficient record" verdict below means, and the Grade F reflects how thin the evidence is. The few related studies DATOM did find appear below, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
It's tempting to read "0 of 4 sources directly support this" as if DATOM were saying the claim is probably false. That's not right. DATOM's confidence score here is 11%, in the "Speculative" band, not 0%. That's an unusual result, and it points in a different direction than you might expect.

Normally, when most of the sources found support a claim, the confidence score can climb higher than the underlying evidence quality alone would justify. Here it's the opposite problem: almost none of the sources found (0% support, and 75% or 3 of 4 only loosely related) actually test the specific thing the claim describes. That near-total gap is what keeps the score low, in the single digits, rather than driving it all the way down to zero. DATOM treats "we didn't find evidence for this exact idea" very differently from "we found evidence and it proves the idea wrong." This is the first case, not the second.

None of the 4 sources actually tested a funding cut of 20% or more tracking closely, at the 0.5 correlation strength the claim specifies, with a coverage drop within two years. So there's nothing here that disproves the claim, just some related material that has to be weighed carefully.

That related material is also not built for creating confidence. The 4 sources used 4 completely different research methods with no overlap between them, so not one single finding here has been confirmed a second time by a different study using a similar approach. Two of the four sources also come with only partial information about how they were built or sourced, including the one study that's from outside the 2010-2020 time period this claim covers. And with only 4 sources total against the 100 DATOM aims to gather for a claim like this, that's just 4% of the volume needed to tell a real pattern apart from noise.

The honest way to read 11% is: not enough has been found here to say anything with real confidence. It is not: the evidence leans against this claim.
decisionSupport: Don't treat this claim's specific funding-to-coverage link as proven: none of the 4 sources DATOM found actually measured it, and DATOM reached just 4% of the 100 sources it was aiming for on this claim.

The one real, solid pattern here is a genuine slowdown in measles vaccine coverage progress, from 70.5% of districts improving between 2000-2010 down to just 40.1% between 2010-2019, across 101 low- and middle-income countries. But the researchers who found it say it was caused by conflict, doubts about vaccines, funding, and supply problems together, not funding cuts on their own. Don't single out funding as the cause.

The Angola example in that same study, health spending per person dropping 28% from 2010-2018 alongside a coverage slowdown, is just one illustrative case inside a larger study. It is not a tested statistical link between funding and coverage.

If you need solid evidence for a real decision, look for studies that directly connect specific funding changes to coverage outcomes over time. None of the 4 studies here, a literature review, a coverage-rate comparison across countries, a case-control household survey, or a geographic modeling study, were built to make that connection.

Don't treat the one source marked 'contradicts' as evidence against this claim. It's marked that way because it's off-topic: it measures how well vaccines prevent antibiotic-treated illness in 65,815 to 944,173 children, not because it found something that disproves a funding-coverage link.
guide.faultLines:
Too Few Sources: DATOM found just 4 sources against a goal of 100 for this claim, only 4% of what's needed. With that little material, there's no way to separate a real pattern from random noise. The low 11% score ("Speculative") is simply the honest math result of that shortfall. It is not a verdict that the claim is false.

No Two Studies Confirm Each Other: the 4 sources used 4 completely different research methods: a policy literature review, a comparison of coverage rates across countries, a case-control household survey, and a geographic modeling study. Because no two sources used a similar method, not one single finding here has been independently double-checked by a comparable study. That's part of why this evidence doesn't add up to a consistent picture.

Wrong Time Period, Wrong Topic: one source (Berman 2004) is from before the 2010-2020 period this claim covers, entirely outside the window. Of the other three, none measures funding levels directly. One (Lewnard 2020) measures how well vaccines prevent illness, not funding. Another (Bruni 2020) measures how many people finish the HPV vaccine series, not funding. And only one study, the Local Burden of Disease Vaccine Coverage Collaborators 2020 measles mapping study, touches funding at all, and even then only as one of four things named together (alongside conflict, doubts about vaccines, and supply problems) behind a documented slowdown, not as something tested on its own.

name: Vaccination Coverage Equity and Health System Financing
plainQuestion: Cutting international vaccine funding causes vaccination coverage rates to drop in low-income countries.
scope: Studies looked at low and middle-income countries, mostly between 2010 and 2019 (one source is from 2004, outside that range). The people studied range from children under 5 to teenagers, and in some cases the age group isn't specified.
metric: How much countries spend on vaccine programs over time, how many children get measles and HPV vaccines, and how many illness cases are prevented by vaccination.
aboutClaim: DATOM found only 4 real sources for this claim, well short of the 100 it aims for. None of them directly tests what the claim says: that a funding cut of 20% or more closely tracks with a national vaccine coverage drop within two years. That's why confidence sits at just 11% ("Speculative"). Of the 4 sources: 0 support the claim, 1 is marked as contradicting it, and 3 are only loosely related. One source is from 2004, before the time period this claim covers. One measures vaccine effectiveness, not funding. One documents a coverage slowdown without any funding data attached to it. And one mentions funding only as one of four things happening together behind a slowdown, not as something tested on its own. What is real here is a genuine, well-documented slowdown in vaccination progress in lower-income countries after 2010. But the sources that found it say it was caused by conflict, doubts about vaccines, supply problems, and funding together, not funding cuts by themselves.
